t: What Effective Classroom Management Really Means ly-means/
q: For many teachers, effective classroom management brings to mind an image of a silent, somber environment.
Effective classroom management isn’t a no-fun, you-against-them proposition. It isn’t a dampening or suppressing of behavior. And it isn’t uptight, tense, or stressful.
It’s about trust and influence. It’s about relationships and leadership. It’s about students behaving and giving their best because they want to, not because they’re forced to.
It includes strictness only in a sense that well-defined boundaries of behavior—whose only goal is to protect learning and enjoyment—are faithfully maintained.
Simply put, effective classroom management is where the desires and fulfillment of both students and teachers meet.
We’ve heard from hundreds of teachers just like you who have put our simple and honest strategies into action and experienced transformational results.

q: Trying and failing to motivate unmotivated students is a common frustration among teachers.
True motivation, however—that which is internal and sustaining—doesn’t develop through convincing. It isn’t about ramped-up enthusiasm or flattery.
The first step is to stop the flow of excessive and over-the-top praise.
You’re going to give plain and honest feedback about the evidence you see on the page or screen.
Now, it’s important to note that it must be true. The least motivated in particular can recognize phoniness from a mile a way.
By truthfully pointing out quality when you see it, you spark their once dormant intrinsic motivational engine to life. You wake up the sleeping giant.
x: Standard motivational advice—praise, encouragement, reward, repeat—is described as largely ineffective with chronically unmotivated students.
True, lasting motivation is framed as intrinsic inspiration rather than something achieved by external convincing or cheerleading.
Step one of the strategy: stop excessive praise, pep-talks, and 'talking students through' their capabilities.
Step two: quietly watch for genuine evidence of quality work and respond with plain, honest, specific observations about the work itself, delivered without an exaggerated tone.
Michael Linsin proposes a strategy for reaching chronically unmotivated students that departs from the usual advice of increased praise, encouragement, and pep talks.

q: The good news is that as long as it was a minor setback, and not a total loss of control, it isn’t difficult to do.
When recovering from a bad day, lining up outside will also send the message that the expectation bar has been picked up off the floor and placed back on the top rung where it belongs.
Rehashing yesterday’s woes is counterproductive. It merely drags the bad energy with you into the morning.
The first routine of the day is critical in restoring your classroom to its well-behaved state. A smooth and efficient performance will put to rest any concerns from the day before.
The biggest mistake teachers make after a bad day is to turn grim and standoffish, to use a show of disappointment and the threat of turning ‘mean’ as a hedge against a repeat performance.
The steps above, however, address the cause of the problems from the day before. They refresh and restore your classroom back to well-being.

t: How To Handle Class-Clown Disruptions And Disrespect -disrespect/
q: The truth is, the most effective classrooms laugh. They laugh and joke and enjoy each other much more than most teachers realize.
But an angry reaction will only make matters worse. It will extend and deepen the interruption. It will bring stress and negativity into your classroom.
The truth is, when they make a silly comment, their intention isn’t to humiliate you. How you feel about it emotionally isn’t even on their radar.
Reacting in anger won’t cut it, not even close. In fact, the most effective reaction is no reaction at all.
You see, when you let the elephant in the room just stand there, alone and awkward and shuffling its feet, the lesson becomes powerful and meaningful to everyone in the class.
In less than 60 seconds you’re back to work. As if it never happened.
x: Humor is framed as a genuine potential asset in the classroom, and the most effective classrooms are described as ones that laugh and enjoy each other, within the bounds of class rules.
An angry reaction to a disruptive joke is said to worsen the disruption, extend the interruption, and damage the teacher-student relationship long-term.
Disruptive jokes or comments that pull the class off task are usually motivated by a student's desire to entertain peers, not to humiliate the teacher personally.
Michael Linsin acknowledges that humor can be a genuine asset in a classroom, but addresses how to handle disruptive jokes or comments that pull the class off task or humiliate the teaching moment.
